1:
The chapter opens with a word the commentators weigh first. Gill notes that the Hebrew particle at the head is not a copulative but a conversive, turning the future tense into the past; without that office the clause would have to be read "the word of the Lord shall come," which would give a wrong sense. He adds that Hebrew books, and historical ones especially, commonly begin in just this way, so the opening implies no lost fragment of some earlier prophecy, and the Targum renders the phrase as a prophecy from the Lord. Ellicott agrees while defending the English: strictly the word is "And," yet the received rendering quite adequately represents the Hebrew manner of beginning a narrative, whether it stands as a book by itself or continues an account already in hand.

Calvin presses the same particle for more. To him it intimates, indirectly, that the prophet had already been called to the teaching office, so that what follows is part of an ordinary function rather than the beginning of one. Calvin then offers a reason for the sending: God, wearied with the obstinacy of his own people, meant to set before them an example of docility in an uncircumcised nation, and so render them the more inexcusable. They professed true religion, yet despised every prophet sent among them, while three days of preaching turned a whole heathen city. He restrains the inference. Some read the mission as a veiled announcement of the future call of the nations; Calvin answers that our Lord confined the comparison to one particular thing, the three days, so that this prophet is a type not because he went out to the Gentiles but because he was brought back to life.

Delitzsch supplies the man. He was born at Gath-hepher in Zebulon, a small hamlet north of Nazareth; he lived under the second Jeroboam and foretold that king's success against the Syrians. That the father's name is the same establishes that the man commissioned here is that prophet, and the mission eastward falls later than the word spoken in the king's favour. Clarke concurs and adds a reckoning: the king came to the throne some eight hundred and twenty-three years before the Christian era and reigned in Samaria forty-one years; as a prophet, Clarke thinks, this man probably had no other errand.

Clarke also draws a line under how the book is to be read. He rehearses the expedients — that the history allegorises Manasseh's imprisonment and release, that the fish was really a ship bearing a sea-creature on its stern, that the swallowing was a dream dreamt in the hold, that the whole is a parable of repentance — and sets against them the appeal our Lord made to the main facts: that there was such a person, that he was preserved alive three days and nights within a sea-creature, and that his preaching turned the Ninevites. That testimony "puts an end to all mythological, allegorical, and hypothetical interpretations of those great facts." In its literal sense alone, he says, he undertakes this book. He notes a Phoenician fable of Hesione chained to a rock and rescued by Hercules from a sea-monster, quoted from Lycophron and the scholiasts; the fable might easily have been taken from the true history, he observes, though some have been ready enough to suggest the reverse.

Henry reads the commission as an honour. His name signifies a dove, a fitting name for those who should be harmless as doves and mourn over the sins of the land; his father's name means "my truth," for prophets should be sons of truth. And the word came to him — was to him, Henry insists, since God's words are substance where the words of men are wind. He had known that voice before and could tell it from a stranger's.
2:
The city is named great, and the commentators take the adjective seriously. Gill makes it the Assyrian metropolis, an ancient foundation of Asshur rather than Nimrod; Strabo allows it larger than Babylon. Clarke reports a compass of four hundred and eighty stadia, some fifty-four English miles, though not all of it was covered with streets, since the circuit took in ground needed to feed the district. From the six score thousand infants he reckons six hundred thousand souls, though such calculations, he grants, are precarious. Ellicott adds that the mounds along the Tigris more than confirm the impression the city made on the ancient world, and that what lies beneath is less a city than a group of cities.

Calvin asks why the greatness is mentioned, and answers that it was spoken for the prophet's sake: the Lord meant to arm him, lest the splendour, wealth and power of the place frighten him out of the errand. Calvin distinguishes the mission from that of Nahum, who prophesied against the same city but stayed at home, comforting a distressed people rather than instructing the Ninevites. The charge to cry against her is likewise hard — an unknown foreigner denouncing destruction on the seat of the world's only monarchy — and Calvin finds its strength in the clause that follows: the prophet contends not as a private man but as a herald summoning the city to God's tribunal.

On the wickedness come up, Clarke sees a personification of evil, ascending from earth to stand before the Supreme Judge and witness against its own delinquency and those it seduced. Ellicott quotes the maxim that every iniquity has its own voice at the hidden judgment seat of God, and observes with Pusey that the Hebrew points especially at evil done to others — the violence the Ninevites themselves afterwards own as their sin.

The flight divides the interpreters. Gill sets Tarshish opposite to the errand — the sea, westward, where the city lay east — and canvasses the candidates: Tarsus in Cilicia, favoured by Josephus and Saadiah Gaon; Tunis; Carthage; Tartessus in Spain. He inclines to Tarsus. Delitzsch and Ellicott settle on Tartessus, Ellicott placing it on the Guadalquivir and drawing the moral that a man ordered to the far north-east made instantly for the farthest west, since between the saintly height and an abyss there is often no middle ground. Calvin is certain it means Cilicia, not the mere sea. Clarke pauses at the port: Joppa, the nearest harbour to Jerusalem, celebrated in fable as the rock where Andromeda was chained and Perseus freed her, and a place of Phoenician traffic where passengers paid a set fare.

As to fleeing from the presence, none will allow the crude sense. Delitzsch takes the phrase as withdrawal from the service of the God-King of Israel and from the land where he manifested himself, not concealment from an omnipresent God; Marck had warned that the other reading attributes gross ignorance to a prophet. Ellicott lists three senses and notes that commentators reject the first as unworthy — yet the man went below deck as though still hiding, and used the same words to sailors who would hear them literally. Calvin presses the repetition: the phrase stands twice, and that emphasis is the prophet's own confession, so that his apologists write childishly. For the cause Calvin proposes novelty, since no prophet had been drawn away to the heathen and even Peter hesitated over a single Gentile; doubt of any fruit, since long labour among a people called from the womb had effected little; and the weakness of flesh that shrank from so hated a message. He was not a log of wood, Calvin says, and no pretence excuses the sin: the call of God holds first place in the conduct of men, and to build elsewhere is to build in the air.
4:
The verb governs the verse, and the commentators stop on it. Gill says the Lord took a wind from his treasures and hurled it — that is what the word signifies — into that sea, into the very part where the ship was riding. Winds are at God's command, raised at his pleasure, servants that obey their orders. It was sent in pursuit, to stop a voyage where the traveller supposed he had got clean away; Gill records a rabbinic tradition that it struck after a single day's sailing. Delitzsch renders the clause as a throwing of a great wind upon the sea, notes that the Greek translators found a fitting word for the swell, and observes that the ship was said to think itself dashed in pieces, an idiom used of lifeless things and amounting to "was very nearly wrecked." Clarke is brief: a storm which, as the sequel shows, came by God's immediate direction, under which they had nearly suffered shipwreck.

Ellicott hears something more particular. The same verb is used later for casting forth, and here it expresses the sudden burst of the weather — a squall struck the ship, on a coast sailors knew to be dangerous. On the ship being like to be broken, he finds in the literal phrase a seaman's way of speaking, to whom his vessel is a living thing with feelings, hopes and fears.

Calvin takes up the same idiom: some treat the ship as standing by metonymy for the mariners, and he cites the reverse figure in the Gospel narrative, where the sailors stand for the ship. He is content with the plainer construction, since common speech agrees at many points with the Hebrew. What he will not concede is chance. The word rendered "sent out" implies force — the same word serves where a javelin is hurled at David and where the Lord threatens to hurl a people out of their land — so the tempest arose not by accident but by fixed purpose. From one storm he draws the general rule: no change in the air, no rain and no tempest at sea, happens by chance; heaven and earth are so governed that nothing occurs unforeseen or undecreed.

He then meets the obvious objection. Is it consistent with reason that a shipload of men should be nearly drowned for the fault of one? Calvin answers that although the Lord had special regard here to a single fugitive, there were hidden reasons why he might justly involve the rest. Many vessels were doubtless at sea that day, given so many harbours and islands; and there is never wanting a reason why any one of us, even the most apparently innocent, might be called before the tribunal. God can so punish one man as to humble some, chastise others for their sins, and try the patience of yet others. It would be preposterous to measure his working by our wisdom; though he may seem severe, he is in truth sparing men.

Henry reads the storm as a pursuer sent after a deserter. God has the winds in his treasure and squeezes them out when he pleases; the wind blows where it wills as far as we are concerned, but not as far as God is, for it blows where he directs. Sin, he notes, brings storms into the soul, the family, the church and the nation, being a disquieting thing. He observes that some read the clause as singling out that ship and no other: other vessels were on the same sea at the same hour, yet this one was tossed beyond the rest. And he turns that to comfort: the tempest was sent to fetch a runaway back to God and to his duty, and it is a great mercy to be called home when we go astray, though the summons come in a storm.
5:
Their terror is evidence. Gill argues that the storm must have been supernatural to frighten men bred to the sea; Calvin agrees, since sailors are a hardy race, and men so hardened were now disquieted with fear. Both note the Hebrew name: it comes from the word for salt, so they are salt-men as ours are sea-men, though Gill records one rabbi's guess that the name came from a cargo of salt. Ellicott, recalling the cry in Shakespeare's Tempest that all is lost and every man to prayers, guesses they were Phoenicians, or a mixed company. Clarke says simply that they were heathens, each with a different object of worship.

Their remedies are read as carefully. Ellicott observes that the word for the goods thrown over is general, covering movables of every sort, while the cargo proper would have been kept till the last extremity, as in the shipwreck Luke describes; "to lighten it of them" means, in the idiom, to give themselves relief. On the hiding place he prefers "recesses" to "sides," and notes that the word rendered "ship" is peculiar to this passage, from a root meaning to cover with boards, so a decked vessel is meant. Clarke takes the jettison as lading thrown over to ride out the weather, and pictures berths below deck like those of our packets.

The sleep draws out the best of them. Ellicott finds it natural that a man fleeing a duty should go below, since to watch the shore recede from the deck would have been mental torture; the slumber is explained by the fatigue of a hurried journey, and by the fact that when a resolution is irrevocably taken conscience ceases its warning while the restlessness of remorse has not yet begun. A brief interval remains, he writes, in which the exile from himself can flee. Clarke thinks him exhausted and overcome with distress, which often ends in heavy sleep, and remembers the disciples in the garden. Calvin allows no such indulgence. The man carried his own executioner in his heart and ought to have trembled even asleep. Every circumstance paints that insensibility: the others running about the deck, stripping themselves of their property and crying to their gods, while the man whose fault had raised the sea lay still.

The officer who wakes him has a title they enjoy. Gill renders it master of the ropers, over sailors who drew the ropes and handled the sails; missing his passenger, he sought him out and found him at the bottom of the vessel. Delitzsch calls him the upper-steersman, chief of those who manage the ship, the name formed from the word for a cable; Ellicott, allowing that Jewish nautical terms are obscure, translates chief of those who work at the rope, and suggests steersmen or topmen, not rowers.

His words are weighed closely. Delitzsch gives them: How canst thou sleep soundly? Arise, call upon thy God; perhaps God will think of us, that we may not perish — the divine name here carrying the article, and so meaning the true God. Ellicott makes the same point and reads the appeal as springing partly from a need of sympathy, as when the disciples woke their Master, partly from belief in a prophet's prayer, and behind that from a sense that the God of Israel was pre-eminently great, rather than superstition lest some deity be overlooked. Calvin makes the moment an indictment of religion without a rule. The pilot could bind him to no standard, since men are always content with a general apprehension of God, each shaping a deity to his fancy. All agree that there is some God and that a dead idol can do nothing; but in the particulars every one is in the dark, inventing a crooked path. Without a certain rule there is no stability, and fictitious worship leaves men in a labyrinth.
7:
Gill supposes the prophet did rise at the master's call and may well have prayed; but the weather held, and the crew then turned to one another. Calvin takes the proposal itself as a measure of the storm. A strong wind is no marvel, and a tempest following it no novelty; something far more dreadful must have been abroad to convince men that God was present as an avenger, for the ungodly recognise vengeance only in extremity. Casting lots was no ordinary expedient of theirs when weather rose; they came to it judging that so unusual a punishment must have some very serious cause. It was, Calvin adds, a proof of extreme fear, since men take to lots only when destitute of judgment and counsel — and here they were partly in error.

Clarke calls the practice a very ancient way of seeking the mind of Divine Providence, and reads it as proof that the sailors supposed some hidden crime aboard. He tells of a philosopher caught at sea in a violent storm, who, when the crew began crying to the gods for safety, said: be silent and cease your prayers, for should the gods learn you are here, we shall all be lost. Whatever the custom's ordinary standing, Clarke holds that here God directed the lot. Ellicott supplies the background. Classical writers as well as the Scriptures illustrate the belief that an impious man's presence draws his companions into indiscriminate ruin, and the feeling was naturally strongest at sea; he quotes the ode in which one who profanes the rites of Eleusis is barred from the poet's house and voyage, since roofs give way and boats are wrecked, and neglected Justice often confounds true men with thieves. Cicero's story of Diagoras is cited to the same effect.

Once the lot has fallen, Calvin observes, they doubt no more than if the man had been convicted a hundred times; the point of the appeal was that what lay hidden should come to light. Two convictions were thus held even by heathens: that God can draw out the truth, and that he presides over what seems most fortuitous. Hence they put questions rather than act. On the first he is careful: the word rendered occupation means not a wrongdoing but a kind of life, a manner of employment; they asked how the man had spent his days, putting each inquiry in due order, though the record compresses them.

The manner of the questioning strikes them as remarkable. Gill notes that they did not fall upon him at once and throw him overboard, as men in their position might well have done, considering what they had suffered and lost on his account; they treat him with great respect, tenderness and lenity, and entreat him. Clarke calls it a very gentle method of bringing the charge home, the several questions giving him the utmost latitude to make the best of his own case. Ellicott finds artistry in the grammar: the peculiar Hebrew idiom for "on whose account" is put more elegantly when the sailors address the prophet than when they used it among themselves a moment before, one of many touches marking the narrative's finish. Some manuscripts omit the repeated question, and some have accordingly treated it as a gloss; but the repetition is natural, since men who see the lot fall on so unsuspicious a person want the verdict confirmed from his own mouth, and the rapid leap from question to question suits their excitement.

Henry draws the moral. When those who profess religion do wrong, they will hear of it from people who make no such profession; and when sin has raised a storm and laid us under the tokens of God's displeasure, the question that matters is what is to be done with the sin that raised it.
9:
The answer is read for its order. Calvin points out that it reverses the questions, taking the last first: the country is named at once, while the enquiry about occupation is met with the words about fearing the Lord — that was his calling, fear including worship and service, and it ought to be every man's work. To the question what evil he had done he returns nothing; Calvin thinks he had told them already, before the weather rose, that he was fleeing. Ellicott judges the recorded reply an abbreviation of what was said.

Why "a Hebrew" and not an Israelite? Gill answers that the Targum wrongly renders it a Jew, which would be false, the man belonging to Zebulun and so to the northern kingdom; nor would he say Israelite, lest he be reckoned among that people's idolatries; the older name was common to both and declared his nation, his religion and his God. Calvin reaches the same end another way: the northern tribes being then mostly idolatrous, the prophet claims descent from the patriarchs, true servants of God and true Hebrews — passengers, sojourners and pilgrims on the earth, as the word imports. Ellicott notes that the original order is more striking, a Hebrew I, and that the Greek translators read a servant of the Lord.

On the confession of the Creator they are warm. Clarke calls this the point where he was faithful, giving honest testimony to the God he served and setting him before the sailors far above the objects of their adoration — the God of heaven, who made sea and dry land and governs both. Ellicott quotes the judgment that the emergency recalls the man to himself, so that the better part of his character appears, his conduct through the rest of the chapter dignified and manly. The words about sea and land mark the change wrought in him, for he feels how futile it was to hide from the maker of everything; but they were spoken for the crew too, who owned the God of Israel as a tribal deity but never as Creator of the world they lived in and the water they sailed on. The storm, Ellicott says, preached the omnipotence of God.

Calvin refuses to let the profession excuse him. One might suppose he was parading his piety to evade the crime; but since the sailors prove to know of the flight, the confession must have been honest, and naming the true God first aggravates the offence rather than lessening it. Had he merely owned the wrong, the fault would have looked smaller; beginning with the framer of heaven makes it monstrous.

The effect on the crew is measured by all. Gill explains their terror: finding him a Hebrew, and the God of the Hebrews angry — one of whom they had heard much and now felt the power — they reasoned that if flight was punished so, and they were guilty of worse, what might be done to them; the destruction he was sent to announce could only deepen it. Delitzsch puts it simply: they feared, in the storm, the wrath of God on account of the prophet's sin. Ellicott insists their question is horror, not curiosity: not why hast thou done this, but what is this that thou hast done. Calvin agrees that it is no request for a reason but an exclamation over the evil, judged by its effects, since they had known of the flight and now saw what it amounted to. Superstitious men entertain strange alarms, then cajole themselves back into ease; these were so smitten that they perceived the God of Israel a righteous judge, not the thing the nations imagined, and gave him his glory. There is a further justice in it: having withdrawn from God's authority, the runaway now finds heathens and barbarians set over him as censors and judges.
11:
Discovery settles nothing. Henry notes that the sea grew more violent still, for when we find sin to be the cause of our troubles and do not forsake it, we make bad worse. So the crew press on, first asking the offender himself. Henry sees in that a recognition that they had a prophet aboard, and would do nothing even in his own case without consulting him; he appeared a delinquent, but a penitent too, and they would neither insult over him nor offer rudeness. We ought, Henry adds, to act with great tenderness towards those overtaken in a fault and brought into distress by it. Perhaps they hoped he could name another expedient; perhaps they meant to show how plain the case was by letting him be his own judge, as he had been his own accuser. Clarke says the same in a sentence: in these poor men there was an uncommon degree of humanity and tender feeling.

Calvin traces the restraint to fear. They dared do nothing, having improved almost in an instant, and spared an Israelite because they now acknowledged that among that people the true God was worshipped. Otherwise, since God was plainly displeased through his fault, why not save themselves at once by so obvious an expiation? Their delay proves that the fear of God held them back. On the words he is exact: the phrase is literally that the sea may cease from upon us, the waves rolling over them; and the sea is said to go when turbulent, as it rests when calm, the verb signifying continuance rather than increase — hardly conceivable in any case, shipwreck being dreaded already. He passes on a striking if fanciful comment: the sea went as commanded, went to manifest the vengeance of its Lord, went to prosecute a runaway prophet, and swelled while the mariners delayed. Ellicott adds that the word rendered calm is used of the lull after a storm and of peace after strife, while the phrase for the raging is literally that it was going and being agitated.

The sentence he passes on himself divides them. Ellicott holds that no prophetic inspiration was needed: the man is too manly to survive at the cost of others, and will not involve his companions in his ruin. Calvin will not have it so. The knowledge cannot have come from the lot, common to all aboard; it came by the prophetic spirit, and from the religion in which he was trained. On that reading he does not merely expect God to be pacified but knows his death will serve as the expiation, so the tempest will subside.

Calvin faces the harder question, whether a man may offer himself to die at all, since to press forward looks like despair. He might have surrendered to their will; instead he stimulates them: there is no other way to pacify God. The answer is that he knew himself doomed, and gave himself up persuaded that he had been summoned by an unmistakable voice. What Calvin most admires is the absence of expostulation: no complaint that the punishment is too severe, but a man bearing his guilt and ascribing to God his honour, with wrath plainly burning against him.

Gill guards the motive. This was no man choosing death rather than the journey he had refused, nor, as one rabbi suggested to the prejudice of his character, one who had overheard the crew planning to throw him over. He was truly sensible of his sin and of deserving such a death, moved by love to men who would else perish through his default, and, knowing the mind of God, submitted cheerfully and in faith, with courage suitable to his office. It would not have been fit for him to leap in and destroy himself; he must die by the hand of justice, the crew being its proper executioners.
13:
Their refusal is noticed first. Clarke says they were unwilling to proceed to such an extremity, and would risk anything rather than cast a disobedient prophet into the deep. Ellicott calls it a fine trait that they would not obey the request until every effort to save the ship was tried, and lingers over the verb: rowed hard renders it well enough but misses the picture, since everywhere else the word describes breaking through a wall. The figure of forcing a vessel through the wave-wall is striking. Henry puts it another way: they rowed against wind and tide, the wind of God's displeasure and the tide of his counsel, and it is vain to think of saving ourselves by any means but destroying our sins.

Calvin reads the reluctance as a change wrought in them. Once the man confessed and refused to escape punishment, these heathens grew anxious to save his life — the more remarkable because each stood in danger from the one who was alone at fault. The Lord so turned their hearts that they saw how grievous a thing it is to flee a divine call. Men reckon this a light offence, but it is not in our power to weigh sins; the balance is false when we estimate our own by our own judgment, and God alone can determine how heavy a fault may be. The episode, Calvin concludes, was meant to make one man an example, that all might know God is to be obeyed as soon as he commands.

When rowing fails they pray, and the commentators dwell on to whom. Gill observes that they cried not to their own gods but to the God of the Hebrews, of whom this providence and the prophet's account had given them some knowledge; and they prayed before laying a hand on him. Clarke says they were now convinced he was the self-existing Being, maker of heaven and earth and author of this storm; and being about to throw a man overboard, they seemed to call God to witness that they did it with the utmost reluctance, and only in obedience. He quotes the Argonautic poem, where a crew debate whether to kill the wretched Medea and cast her as prey to the fishes to avert their own fate.

Ellicott finds in the prayer the contrast running through the book, between the readiness of the heathen to receive religious impressions and the stubbornness of Israel. The plea about this man's life means for taking it, retaliation being as familiar a law to them as to the Hebrews; the closing clause is more impressive in the original — for Thou, Jehovah, as it hath pleased Thee, Thou hast done. The storm, the lot and the prophet's request showed the sailors to be only instruments of a purpose not their own.

Calvin takes the same words as a witness to conscience. The particles are those of entreaty, the sense being that God would not impute to them the slaughter of a just man; the repetition shows their earnestness. Their long toil at the oar is now explained: they were persuaded that this passenger was a prophet of the true God, and pious fear held them back. They saw that he already stood at God's tribunal and that punishment was required, and still wished to preserve his life. Calvin draws a general rule from it. There is implanted by nature in every man an abhorrence of cruelty; however sanguinary men become, they cannot rid themselves of the sense that shedding human blood is hateful. So sailors who hardly retained a drop of humanity fled to God as suppliants when a man's death was in question, taught by nature alone that human blood is precious in his sight. Henry says it in a phrase: even natural conscience cannot but dread blood-guiltiness.
15:
Gill notes that they brought him up out of the hold, the plural mattering, since more than one was employed; it was done not against his will but by his direction. Calvin fastens on what followed. Had the sea gone down after an interval, the calm might have been ascribed to chance; because it rested instantly, nothing could be said except that this man stood condemned by God's judgment. He was thrown in by human hands, yet God so presided that nothing was chargeable to the men beyond executing a sentence he had openly demanded. Delitzsch says the same: the sudden change proved the weather had come entirely on the prophet's account, and the sailors had shed no innocent blood.

What they do next divides the readers. Gill takes their fear to be no longer natural but religious — not a servile dread of punishment but reverence, since they had seen God's power in raising and stilling the tempest and his goodness in sparing them. Clarke goes further: the sacrifice was perhaps the first ever offered aboard a vessel since the ark floated on the deluge, and it is most probable that these heathens became sincere converts. Ellicott is cautious: there may have been live-stock aboard fit for the purpose, but the offering could only be completed on shore, which is why vows were added. Delitzsch insists it was made at once, on the ship, the vows promising more at port.

Calvin refuses the warmer reading. He grants that the proper name of God is used here, marking a difference from the superstitions each man had cried to before. But Scripture uses fear sometimes for outward worship and sometimes for true piety, and there is besides a servile fear that would gladly unseat God while unable to escape his power. Here the Lord extorted a confession in the moment; it was no thorough conversion making new men. If any made no progress, their knowledge only condemned them, since they went on mingling old superstitions with the worship they had come to acknowledge.

On the creature that swallowed him, the verb comes first. Ellicott says the pluperfect misleads: the word means appointed, as it is used later of the gourd, the worm and the east wind, and implies no preparation, still less a creature made for the purpose. Gill likewise denies the rabbinic notion that the fish was formed at the creation for this office, reading the verb of a providence that brought it alongside with its mouth open.

As to what the fish was, none will have a whale. Clarke observes that its throat can scarcely admit a man's leg, and proposes the shark, which abounds in that sea and has a mouth and stomach exceedingly capacious, known to swallow men overboard. Delitzsch argues the same and adds that the true shark reaches twenty-five feet and carries some four hundred lance-shaped teeth in six rows. Gill notes that the Greek word rendered whale must cover all great fishes, and mentions the dog-fish of the fable in which a hero spent three days inside a sea-monster — a story he suspects was borrowed from this history. Ellicott notes that in early Christian painting the monster appears as a huge dragon, but warns that until the prior question is settled — whether the book is literal history, an apologue, or a parable outright — the whole disquisition about the fish looks, as an old commentator said, vain and useless.

Calvin asks what those days were like. A man who had served God faithfully is cast out as unworthy of the common light and cut off from human society, a punishment once reserved for parricides. He had slept in the hold; now God dragged him to his tribunal, and he underwent a continual execution, not killed outright but left to languish. No one, Calvin says, can comprehend what passed through that mind.
